title: Jazz origins and the risk of young people thinking it was white
summary: Johnston worries about college jazz workshops teaching jazz as white; McPartland restates the African-European wedding.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: As I say Helen, that was my brother and myself our first contact with what we call jazz now. Those eight blind men singing spirituals.

One of the reasons I said do you think, asked you whether that group was a negro group or not was that I have observed with the now jazz workshops that are being held in the various colleges around the Country. And Stan Kenton for example is perhaps the person most in demand for giving these jazz workshops. And the purpose of them is supposed to be to teach young people, particularly young white people, about jazz. And as I see it, these other things and from the proposals which I have read for the National Endowment for instance, we are going to have a whole generation of young people who will eventually believe that jazz was entirely white. In our (knowledge?) (it was) only white association. in origin

Now the young musicians of course know better. But I'm talking about these young, uninformed people from colleges in the Middle West and so forth who are learning all about jazz for the first time from......
To me, in my opinion, American jazz music is a wedding between the African negro rhythms and the European harmonies and melodic line. That's a wedding between the two.
But it was the Africans who brought the rhythm over here.
And then of course, as he became acclimated to his new environment you see, he developed the.....
Well you take a white person like myself, I picked up on that. I know that I picked up on the spirituals and then when I heard the jazz, there it was.
Of course. You improvised the blues. That's it. All you do is improvise. Sometimes you know, people play a melody or something, da de da, you know, 'St. Louis Blues.'
